messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Delivery Driver
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 46

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Negative Appraisals: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rajan Mehta is a 34-year-old South Asian American man who works as a delivery driver and has been married for six years. He presented for an initial psychological evaluation approximately four months after a road accident in which he accidentally struck a cyclist while making a right turn in his delivery van. The cyclist, a young woman, sustained a fractured pelvis and a serious head injury and spent several weeks in intensive care. Rajan was not cited for reckless driving — the turn was legal, his speed was within limits, and an investigation found no mechanical fault — but none of that has mattered much to how he understands what happened.

On the afternoon of the accident, Rajan had been running behind schedule. He had checked his mirrors before turning, but the cyclist had been in a blind spot created by the van's wide A-pillar, and by the time he registered the impact — a sound he describes as something between a thud and a crack — it was already over. He pulled over, called 911, and knelt beside the woman on the road, pressing his jacket against a wound on her head while he waited for the ambulance. He remembers her breathing in short, uneven pulls and the way her helmet had split along one side. He stayed until paramedics arrived and took over. He has replayed those minutes thousands of times since.

In the weeks that followed, Rajan returned to work because the household depended on his income, but his experience behind the wheel changed profoundly. Cyclists appearing in his peripheral vision — at intersections, along bike lanes, emerging from side streets — became moments of acute alarm. The sound of his own turn signal, which he now associates with the sequence of events leading up to the impact, produces a tightening in his chest that he cannot fully explain and cannot fully ignore. His sleep has been fragmented, with intrusive images surfacing in the dark: the split helmet, the sound, her irregular breathing. He has started taking longer routes that avoid the intersection where the accident occurred, adding sometimes forty minutes to his working day, and he has told his dispatcher that a particular delivery zone is "too congested," a story that has held so far but one he worries will eventually cost him the route.

What organises Rajan's distress most powerfully is not fear of future accidents but a settled conviction about his own culpability and his own inadequacy. He is certain that the accident happened because of how he acted that day — that a more careful driver, a more attentive man, would have seen her. He does not experience this as bad luck or as a tragic convergence of circumstances. He experiences it as evidence of a failure that was his alone to prevent. Layered on top of this is a grief about what he did not do in the moments before the impact: he had not double-checked the blind spot a second time, had not waited an extra beat. He had the chance to stop what happened and he did not take it, and he has come to believe that this is something he will carry without resolution. When his wife tries to reassure him — pointing to the investigation findings, reminding him that the paramedics said he had helped stabilise the woman — he listens politely and feels nothing shift. The reassurances arrive in a language he can no longer translate into something he believes about himself.

His marriage has been quietly strained. Rajan has become withdrawn in the evenings, sitting with his phone rather than talking, and his wife has begun asking whether something is wrong in a tone that suggests she already suspects the answer. He has not told her the full extent of what he is experiencing, in part because articulating it feels like burdening her and in part because he is not sure she would understand why the legal findings have done nothing to relieve him.

What finally brought him to seek help was a near-miss at an intersection three weeks ago — a cyclist who crossed safely but who left Rajan parked on the shoulder for twenty minutes, unable to continue driving. He has come to therapy not entirely sure what he is hoping for, but most afraid that what he feels about himself on the day of the accident is simply the truth, and that no amount of talking will change it.
